Photographer Tyler Stalman is back with his annual iPhone camera review. Below are his thoughts on the iPhone 18 Pro's new variable aperture, Photographic Styles, Apple Reference Image, and more.

Stalman dives into the iPhone 18 Pro camera's variable aperture

While this year's iPhone 18 Pro brings several new features, including a 2nm A20 Pro chip, a new vapor chamber, and a smaller Dynamic Island, the biggest camera upgrade is arguably the new variable aperture system.

Also new this year are updates to Cinematic mode, expanded Photographic Styles with new Texture controls, Apple Reference Image, and further refinements to the Camera app's pro controls.

Today, photographer Tyler Stalman shared his review of all the new hardware and software features of the iPhone 18 Pro, adding to the wave of reviews dropping alongside the lifting of the embargo, including our own.

Stalman notes that while he loved the Cosmic Orange color of the iPhone 17 Pro last year, the color tended to show up in reflections when shooting through glass. As such, he suggests pro photographers may opt for the Wine Red or Black, as those colors are less likely to throw off unwanted color in photos or videos.

He also makes it clear from the start that his review compares the iPhone 18 Pro camera to the iPhone 15 Pro, while the review video itself is shot almost entirely on an iPhone 17 Pro.

When it comes to the main camera upgrade, the new variable aperture, Stalman says its addition is "a small step towards making (iPhone) a serious camera."

He also mentions that the wider f/1.48 aperture lets more light hit the sensor, helping reduce ISO in low light and lessening the need for Night mode.

This portion of the review includes some great photos of the aperture blades opening and closing, with Stalman pointing out that Apple's design is rather unique, placing the aperture blades above the main lens element rather than deeper within the lens like a traditional camera lens.

Stalman also says that the iPhone 18 Pro's 4x zoom (which last year's iPhone also had) is a major improvement over the iPhone 16 Pro's 5x zoom, which sometimes felt a little too tight.

Speaking of things that may go too far, he also briefly touches on the new AI editing tools, like Clean Up, Extend, and Re-Frame, noting that while they're technically impressive and look convincing, they can make such major changes that the resulting image no longer fully matches the feel of the original photo.

Moving on to the iPhone 18 Pro's new Texture options, including Smooth Skin, Glow, and Film, Stalman demonstrates each by adjusting the strength from 0 to 100. As for his thoughts, he says the Smooth Skin effect subtly reduces skin detail without simply blurring the skin, while the Glow effect offers a diffused highlight look similar to a black pro-mist filter.

He was also impressed by the grain and halation of the Film effect, although he wishes Apple offered more options to control the amount of grain.

The review also covers Apple Reference Image, iPhone Cinematic mode (and why Stalman still recommends Apple Log for truly cinematic footage), the new Apple Log 2, and naturally weaves in photo and video comparisons between the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro.
